title: What went right this week: a brighter future for Kosovo, plus more
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
What went right this week: a brighter future for Kosovo, plus more

Kosovo was cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting oil, and a new species was discovered, plus more
The post What went right this week: a brighter future for Kosovo, plus more appeared first on Positive News.

Actual Article Body:
Kosovo was finally cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting fossil fuels, and a new cat species was discovered, plus more good news

Kosovo was finally cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting fossil fuels, and a new cat species was discovered, plus more good news

Some 27 years after the Kosovo War ended, a humanitarian mission to clear the country of landmines has concluded.

The Halo Trust, a mine-clearance charity, announced this week that its work in the country was done, claiming the cleared land has “paved the way for Kosovo’s recovery”.

More than 800,000 people were displaced during the Kosovo War (1998-1999). When refugees returned home, they found a ravage landscape littered with mines. According to the Halo Trust, 150 people were killed or injured by mines in the first month alone.

Kosovo is a different place today. Cleared land has paved the way for agriculture and infrastructure projects, helping the country’s post-war economy to flourish. According to the World Bank, average life expectancy is now 78 – just one year less than it is in the US.

“Kosovo shows us that the real impact of removing landmines and cluster bombs is not measured in hectares cleared, but in what that land makes possible over time,” said Atholl Stewart, programme manager for Halo Kosovo.

Halo’s workers from Kosovo are now leading the charity’s operations in Syria and Ukraine.

Image: uskarp

The global goal to protect 30% of the planet by 2030 is within reach, but governments must accelerate action to achieve it.

That’s according to a major review of the policy, published this week. It found that around 20% of land and inland waters are already designated protected. Existing commitments, it adds, would increase that to 27% by 2030 – just shy of the target.

“Real progress is being made,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature. “Countries have expanded protected and conserved areas around the world – safeguarding critical ecosystems such as forests, wetlands, and mangroves.”

However, the Global Assessment 30×30 report warns that progress at sea is much slower. It finds that just 10% of the ocean is designated protected – a gap authors say could be closed by the High Seas Treaty (more on that below), which gives nations new powers to protect waters outside of their national boundaries.

Enforcing protected areas is another challenge. The report warns that bottom trawling and other damaging practices are still happening in many conservation zones.

O’Donnell called on governments to accelerate action and reframe the 30×30 target “not only as a conservation imperative, but as an investment in economic resilience, climate stability, food and water security, health, and long-term prosperity”.

Image: iStock

“The world is uniting around ocean protection even in divided times,” campaigners said this week, as the number of nations to ratify the High Seas Treaty reached 100.

Australia, Brunei, Canada, Germany, Papua New Guinea and Zimbabwe are the latest countries to ratify the treaty, which entered force in January. It provides the world’s first legal framework to conserve life on the high seas, which covers nearly half the planet’s surface. Currently, less than 1% of international waters are fully protected.

“In many cultures, the number 100 carries real weight – whether it is a marker for age, an anniversary, or a symbol of luck and prosperity. For the High Seas Treaty, it marks the real momentum of the world uniting around ocean protection, even in divided times,” said Rebecca Hubbard, director of the High Seas Alliance.

Hubbard called on more countries to ratify, and urged those that have done so to turn the “wave of support turns into real decisions”.
